title: Comparing the complexity of wayfinding tasks in built environments

findings.mechanism: higher number of decision points, poor clues, and no clues in Frankfurt compared to Vienna
findings.quote: The wayfinding task 'going from the departure hall to the gate' has a higher rating of points within 'problem areas' at Frankfurt International (2) than at Vienna International (1).

findings.consequent: number of decision points in wayfinding task
findings.mechanism: decision points require choices, increasing difficulty
findings.quote: Frankfurt has more decision points (10) than Vienna (5).

findings.consequent: number of poor clues in wayfinding task
findings.mechanism: poor clues do not reassure people, leading to hesitation
findings.quote: The sum of all 'poor' clues totals 14 in Frankfurt and only 5 in Vienna.

findings.consequent: number of no clues in wayfinding task
findings.mechanism: no clues lead to people getting lost
findings.quote: The sum of all missing clues totals 7 in Frankfurt and only 3 in Vienna.

stimuli.description: sequences of color slides simulating a route-following task from departure hall to a specific gate at Vienna International Airport and Frankfurt International Airport

limitations: The demonstration of our method is based only on a few interviews.
A more sophisticated and extended experimental design is needed to verify the cross-cultural universality of image-schematic representations.
Instead of using slides to interview people about their spatial experiences, one could test human subjects in real-world application space.
Interviews should be conducted for different built environments, such as public transport buildings, hospitals, or libraries.
Many image schemata are not experienced in isolation but are correlated with other image schemata—represented as tightly coupled image-schematic blocks.
It has to be established which image schemata are relevant for the comparison of wayfinding tasks in built environments.
